newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to extradite suspected ETA member to Spain.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to extradite suspected ETA member to Spain.

text.p: During an official visit from the king and queen of Spain, Mexico said that suspected Basque terrorists will not be granted haven, approving late on Friday the extradition to Spain of a member of the separatist group ETA.

While King Juan Carlos was applauding Mexican-Spanish cooperation in cracking down on suspected terrorists and drug traffickers before a meeting of the Mexican Senate, a Mexican federal judge authorised the extradition of suspected Basque ETA separatist Oscar Cadenas Lorente.

Mexico's state-owned news agency Notimex reported late on Friday that Judge Armando Baez Espinoza, a federal district judge in Toluca, west of Mexico City, approved Spain's request to extradite Cadenas Lorente.

The two countries on Friday also applauded modifications made last year aimed at expediting extraditions. An extradition treaty between Mexico and Spain was signed in 1978, a year after the re-establishment of diplomatic ties.
The new procedures target the declared arch-enemies of each government, the Basque separatists in Spain and international drug traffickers in Mexico.

"Without a doubt (the new extradition protocols) will be a valuable aid in the task of defending our peoples against scourges and contemporary threats, like terrorism, that overrun borders," the king told Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo during a formal dinner.

Cadenas Lorente, alias "El Guero" (The Blond), is wanted in Spain on charges of attempted murder, causing criminal damage and belonging to an armed band. He has also been named as a suspect in a 1995 kidnapping by ETA. He was arrested last December on a warrant issued by Spain.
Cadenas Lorente began a hunger strike following the judge's decision, his lawyers told the Mexico City daily La Jornada. The lawyers added that that they would appeal the Mexican judge's decision.
ETA, Basque Homeland and Freedom in the Basque language, seeks an independent homeland from Spain, often using violent methods such as bombing in its campaign.

Spain has labeled the group terrorist and goes to great ends to ferret out suspected ETA members who seek refuge abroad. Mexico extradited three other ETA suspects to Spain last year after a visit by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
"The terrorists have converted their prolonged murderous activity into their only reason for being," King Juan Carlos said.
ETA has killed some 800 people since starting a drive for Basque independence in 1968.
The Mexican move to turn over Cadena Llorentes was well received on Saturday by Madrid.

"Everything that means collaboration, as long as it's fully legal, for better conditions in the fight against terrorism, will always be judged positively by the Spanish government," Labour Minister Javier Arenas told journalists.

In ceremonies marking the start of the King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia's visit on Friday, the king and Zedillo both went to great pains to marvel at the high level of Spanish-Mexican cooperation and mutual admiration.

On Saturday, the king and queen were given the keys to Mexico City by Mayor Oscar Espinosa Villareal, and the royal couple planned to visit important cultural and architecural sites later on Saturday and on Sunday.
On Monday, they will inaugurate an unprecented conference on the Spanish language in the north-central city of Zacatecas.
